The lorry had been stuck in the mud since morning. Its driver, a thin man with a cap pushed back on his head, sat on the bonnet smoking and watching the sky as if it owed him money. Around him the passengers had arranged themselves according to their temperaments. The traders argued; the students slept; an old woman in a blue wrapper sat upright on her basket of kola and stared at the road ahead with the patience of someone who had waited for worse things than lorries. questions.explanation: Temperament is a person's nature; the traders argue, the students sleep and so on.

My grandfather's room smelt of snuff and old paper. He kept everything: letters from children who were now grandparents, receipts from shops that had long since closed, a photograph of himself as a young clerk, stiff and proud in a white shirt that must have been borrowed. The town council had promised a new bridge for eleven years. Each election season, surveyors in yellow helmets appeared at the river with tripods and measuring tapes, and each election season the people cheered. The surveyors were photographed, the photographs appeared in the newspapers, and the surveyors went away. Meanwhile, the children continued to cross the river on the old plank, holding their shoes above their heads in the rains. When at last a foundation stone was laid, a band played, three chiefs made speeches, and the councillor unveiled a brass plate bearing his own name in letters larger than the name of the river. The plate is still there. It is very well polished. The plank is still there too.

questions.stem: Examine the importance of Enobarbus to the structure and meaning of Antony and Cleopatra. [25 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Enobarbus as Antony's loyal friend and blunt soldier who speaks the truth to him (e.g. on Fulvia's death, on fighting by sea)
4 marks: as commentator/chorus: his comments guide the audience's judgement of Antony, Cleopatra and the Romans
4 marks: his celebrated description of Cleopatra on the barge at Cydnus and 'Age cannot wither her' convey her magnetism
4 marks: his desertion to Caesar shows the collapse of Antony's fortunes; Antony's generosity in sending his treasure leads to Enobarbus's remorse and death
5 marks: Relevant, accurate reference to incidents in the play
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Enobarbus is Antony's close companion, a plain-speaking soldier whose cynical wit punctures pretence. He functions like a chorus, commenting on events and characters; through him the audience sees Cleopatra's power most vividly in the barge speech and in his tribute to her 'infinite variety'. He warns against fighting at sea and judges Antony's decline realistically. When he finally deserts to Caesar, Antony's magnanimity in sending his treasure after him breaks his heart, and he dies of remorse, a moving testimony to Antony's greatness even in defeat.

questions.stem: 'Cleopatra is a woman of infinite variety.' Examine the character of Cleopatra in the light of this statement. [25 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: her charm and wit: she captivates Antony and everyone who meets her (barge description, teasing of Antony)
4 marks: her moods and changeability: playful, jealous, cunning, theatrical (e.g. sending word that she is sad when he is merry, striking the messenger)
4 marks: her political shrewdness and self-interest (insisting on fighting at sea, dealings with Thidias, holding back treasure)
4 marks: her genuine love and nobility in death: grief at Antony's death, refusal to be led in Caesar's triumph, dignified suicide
5 marks: Relevant, accurate reference to incidents in the play
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Cleopatra is endlessly changeable: she flirts, sulks, rages and jests in turn, deliberately crossing Antony's moods to hold his attention. She can be cruel (beating the messenger), vain and calculating, and her flight at Actium causes Antony's defeat. Yet her love is real: she mourns Antony passionately, and, rather than be paraded in Rome, she dies regally by the asp, 'Give me my robe, put on my crown'. Her variety makes her one of Shakespeare's most complex heroines.

questions.stem: Examine the theme of racial prejudice in To Kill a Mockingbird. [25 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: Tom Robinson's trial: an innocent black man convicted because of the colour of his skin despite clear evidence
4 marks: the attitudes of the white community: the lynch mob at the jail, the Ewells, the children taunted because Atticus 'defends' a black man
4 marks: Atticus as the voice of justice and equality, defending Tom and teaching his children tolerance
4 marks: consequences: Tom's death; the effect on Jem and Scout; the mockingbird symbol of destroyed innocence

4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Prejudice dominates Maycomb. Although Atticus proves that Tom Robinson, whose left arm is crippled, could not have beaten Mayella, the all-white jury convicts him. A mob tries to lynch Tom, Scout and Jem are mocked because their father defends a black man, and Tom is later shot trying to escape. Atticus represents conscience and justice, teaching his children to see from other people's point of view. Tom, like Boo Radley, is a 'mockingbird' destroyed by a prejudiced society.

questions.stem: Discuss Atticus Finch as a father and as a member of the Maycomb community. [25 marks]

4 marks: his moral courage: accepting Tom Robinson's defence knowing the cost; facing the mob at the jail

questions.explanation: Atticus is a widower who raises Scout and Jem with honesty and gentle discipline, teaching them empathy and courage through example. He defends Tom Robinson, though he knows he will lose, because his conscience demands it, and he sits outside the jail to protect Tom from a mob. His modesty is shown when he shoots the mad dog, a skill his children never knew he had. Though some townspeople despise him, Maycomb trusts him to do its unpleasant duties, and he stands as the moral centre of the novel.

questions.explanation: The Inspector arrives during the engagement celebration and, by questioning each character in turn, reveals how Arthur, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling and Eric all contributed to the girl's death. He controls the action and speaks Priestley's socialist message that we are all responsible for one another. After he leaves, it seems he was no real inspector, yet the closing phone call suggests a supernatural or moral force. He separates the young, who learn, from the old, who refuse to change.

questions.stem: How does Priestley use dramatic irony in An Inspector Calls, and to what effect? [25 marks]

4 marks: irony in the investigation: Mrs Birling demands punishment for the father of the child, not knowing it is Eric
4 marks: effect: makes the older generation look foolish and complacent; strengthens the message of social responsibility; creates suspense
5 marks: Relevant, accurate reference to incidents in the play
4 marks: Organisation and expression: clear introduction, logically developed paragraphs, conclusion; correct, fluent English
questions.explanation: Writing in 1945 about 1912, Priestley lets the audience know what Birling cannot: the Titanic sank, two world wars came, and the old social order collapsed. Birling's boasts thus discredit him and his selfish philosophy. In Act Two, Mrs Birling insists that the young man responsible must be made an example of, while the audience increasingly suspects that it is Eric. The irony creates suspense, exposes hypocrisy and drives home the theme of collective responsibility.

questions.explanation: More and Rich are moral opposites. More, though he loves life and his family, refuses to compromise his conscience and dies for it. Rich begins as a hungry young scholar seeking employment; More advises him to become a teacher, but Rich wants fame. He is gradually corrupted by Cromwell, betrays More and finally commits perjury, for which he is made Attorney-General for Wales. More's remark, 'for Wales!', sums up the contrast between integrity and self-seeking.

Vivid imagery and a regretful tone convey the loss of sincerity that comes with adulthood and modern society.

questions.explanation: Chauntecleer, the proud cock, dreams of a beast that threatens him, but Pertelote persuades him to ignore it. When the fox flatters him about his father's singing, he shuts his eyes to crow and is seized. On the way to the woods he flatters the fox in turn, urging him to boast to his pursuers; the fox opens his mouth and Chauntecleer escapes. The cock vows never again to close his eyes to flattery, the fox resolves never to speak when he should keep silent: the tale warns against pride, flattery and carelessness.

questions.stem:
Read the poem below carefully and answer the questions that follow.

The Night Bus

The night bus coughs at the edge of town,
Its one good headlamp searching the road;
Inside, the tired faces nod
Like heavy fruit on a bending bough.

A baby wakes and is hushed again,
A trader counts her coins by touch,
The driver hums a song of rain
And grips the wheel as if it were a crutch.

We do not speak; we are strangers here,
Yet the same dark carries us all,
And the same thin light, the same slow fear,
And the same hope at the journey's end.

(a) What is the poem about? [5 marks]
(b) Identify and comment on two figures of speech in the poem. [8 marks]
(c) What is the mood of the poem? [4 marks]
(d) Comment on the theme expressed in the last stanza. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) a night journey by bus; tired passengers, a trader, a baby, the driver; strangers sharing the journey
8 marks: (b) any two well explained, 4 marks each: personification ('coughs', 'searching'); simile ('like heavy fruit on a bending bough' - drooping heads); simile ('as if it were a crutch' - the driver's dependence/tiredness); repetition ('the same')
4 marks: (c) weary, quiet, subdued, yet with a note of tenderness and hope
8 marks: (d) common humanity/solidarity: strangers share the same darkness, fear and hope; life as a shared journey (explained with reference to the lines)
questions.explanation: (a) The poem describes a night bus leaving town and the weary passengers inside it. (b) 'The night bus coughs' personifies the old bus as a sick person; 'nod / Like heavy fruit on a bending bough' is a simile for drooping, sleepy heads. (c) Weary and hushed, with a quiet tenderness. (d) Although the passengers are strangers, they share the same darkness, fear and hope: the bus becomes an image of human life as a common journey.

questions.stem:
Read the poem below carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Rain on the Tin Roof

All night the rain drums on the roof,
A thousand fingers, soft, then loud,
As if the sky had stories too
And told them to the sleeping crowd.

My brother sleeps; my mother prays;
The water whispers at the door;
The old roof groans like an old man
Who has heard all these tales before.

And I, awake, lie listening, glad
Of walls, of blankets, of the sound,
While somewhere, under the same sky,
Someone has no roof to be found.

(a) Describe the setting of the poem. [4 marks]
(b) Comment on the use of sound imagery in the first two stanzas. [8 marks]
(c) What contrast is drawn in the last stanza, and what does it reveal about the speaker? [8 marks]
(d) Identify the rhyme scheme of the first stanza. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) a home at night during heavy rain; the family inside (brother asleep, mother praying), a tin roof
8 marks: (b) drumming rain, 'a thousand fingers, soft, then loud' (metaphor of drumming fingers), water 'whispers', roof 'groans': personification and onomatopoeic words create a vivid soundscape (4 marks for each of two well-explained examples)
8 marks: (c) the speaker's comfort and gratitude versus the homeless person exposed to the same rain (4); reveals compassion, thoughtfulness, awareness of privilege (4)
5 marks: (d) abcb (roof/loud/too/crowd: only lines 2 and 4 rhyme)
questions.explanation: (a) A family home with a tin roof on a rainy night. (b) The rain drums like a thousand fingers, the water whispers, the roof groans like an old man: personification and sound words make the night audible. (c) The speaker's warmth and safety are contrasted with someone homeless under the same sky, revealing gratitude and compassion. (d) abcb: 'loud' rhymes with 'crowd'.

questions.stem:
Read the passage below carefully and answer the questions that follow.

The new headmaster arrived on a Monday, in a car so old that the pupils at the gate thought at first it was being pushed. He climbed out, a short man with a large umbrella, though the sky was clear, and stood for a long time looking at the school: the broken louvres, the grass that had swallowed the football field, the signboard on which someone had painted a moustache over the founder's portrait. Then he did a strange thing. He took off his jacket, folded it neatly over the umbrella, picked up a cutlass that a labourer had left against the wall, and began to cut the grass. By the time the bell rang for assembly, half the senior class was cutting with him, and nobody could remember who had started it.

(a) What is the narrative point of view of the passage? [3 marks]
(b) What impression of the school's condition does the passage give? Refer to two details. [6 marks]
(c) What does the headmaster's 'strange thing' reveal about his character? [6 marks]
(d) Comment on the use of humour in the passage. [5 marks]
(e) Comment on the last sentence. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) third-person narration (an outside narrator)
6 marks: (b) neglected and run-down (2); any two details: broken louvres, overgrown football field, defaced signboard (2 each)
6 marks: (c) leads by example, humble, practical, hardworking, unconcerned with status (any two well explained, 3 each)
5 marks: (d) the car so old it seemed pushed; the umbrella under a clear sky; the moustache on the founder's portrait: gentle humour that makes the headmaster likeable
5 marks: (e) his example inspired the pupils spontaneously; leadership by action rather than words; 'nobody could remember who had started it' shows how naturally the change happened
questions.explanation: (a) Third person. (b) The school is neglected: broken louvres, a field swallowed by grass, a defaced signboard. (c) He is humble and practical and leads by example. (d) Gentle humour in the ancient car, the umbrella under a clear sky and the painted moustache makes the scene lively. (e) His action spreads naturally: the pupils join him without being ordered, showing the power of example.

questions.explanation: (a) A tragedy is a serious drama showing the downfall of a great or noble person, usually ending in death. (b) It has a hero of high status (Antony, a triumvir); a tragic flaw (his passion for Cleopatra); a reversal of fortune (defeat at Actium) and recognition; and it arouses pity and fear, leaving the audience purged (catharsis) when the hero dies.

(b) Explain any three elements of prose fiction. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) length (novel long, short story brief, often read at one sitting); scope (novel many characters, subplots, wide time span; short story few characters, single incident/effect); development (novel develops characters fully; short story focuses on a single impression) (any well-explained distinctions)
5 marks: (b) plot: the arrangement of events in a story
5 marks: (b) characterisation: how characters are created and presented
5 marks: (b) setting / point of view / theme / style (any third element well explained)
questions.explanation: (a) A novel is a long work of prose fiction with many characters, subplots and a wide span of time, allowing full development of characters; a short story is brief, focuses on one or two characters and a single incident, and aims at one unified effect. (b) Plot is the sequence of events; characterisation is the presentation of people in the story; setting is the time and place of the action (point of view or theme also acceptable).
